name: Katherine Johnson
bio: Katherine Johnson was an American mathematician whose calculations of orbital mechanics at NASA were critical to the success of the first and later U.S. crewed spaceflights. NASA calls her one of the first African American women to work as a NASA scientist.
clues: I started high school when I was just 10 years old.
In 1939 I was one of the first Black students to integrate West Virginia University's graduate school.
Before his 1962 orbit of Earth, astronaut John Glenn asked for me to double-check the computer's numbers by hand.
My work at NASA was told in the 2016 film Hidden Figures.

name: Alan Turing
bio: Alan Turing was a British mathematician who laid the foundations of computer science and helped break German codes during World War II. He was prosecuted for being gay and was pardoned long after his death.
clues: I was a serious long-distance runner, nearly fast enough to try out for the Olympics.
In 1936 I described an imaginary machine that could carry out any calculation that can be written as steps.
During World War II I helped break Germany's Enigma code at Bletchley Park.
A famous test for whether a machine can think is named after me.

name: Ada Lovelace
bio: Ada Lovelace was an English mathematician who wrote about Charles Babbage's planned Analytical Engine, an early design for a computer. She saw that the machine could do much more than arithmetic, and she is often called the first computer programmer.
clues: My father was a famous poet, but my mother made sure I studied math.
I worked with Charles Babbage on his design for a machine called the Analytical Engine.
I wrote that a computing machine could work with symbols and even music, not just numbers.
I'm often called the first computer programmer.

name: Stephen Hawking
bio: Stephen Hawking was an English physicist who studied black holes and the origin of the universe. He had ALS, which slowly paralyzed him, and he spoke using a computer voice. His book A Brief History of Time made big ideas about space understandable to millions of readers.
clues: For 30 years I held the same professorship at Cambridge that Isaac Newton once held.
I showed that black holes should slowly give off radiation.
I wrote the bestselling book A Brief History of Time.
I used a wheelchair and spoke through a computer-generated voice.

name: Florence Price
bio: Florence Price was an American composer and the first African American woman recognized as a symphonic composer. In 1933 the Chicago Symphony Orchestra performed her Symphony in E minor, the first work by a Black woman played by a major American orchestra. She wrote more than 300 pieces of music.
clues: I grew up in Little Rock, Arkansas, and studied at the New England Conservatory of Music.
I wrote more than 300 pieces, including four symphonies.
In 2009, a big collection of my lost music was found in my abandoned summer house.
I was the first Black woman to have a symphony performed by a major American orchestra.

name: Dolores Huerta
bio: Dolores Huerta is a labor leader who co-founded the National Farm Workers Association with Cesar Chavez, which became the United Farm Workers. She has spent decades fighting for farmworkers' rights, and some credit her with the slogan “Sí se puede” (“Yes, we can”).
clues: I was an elementary school teacher before I became an organizer.
With Cesar Chavez, I co-founded a union for farmworkers.
During the 1965 Delano grape strike, I organized grape boycotts on the East Coast.
Some credit me with the slogan “Sí se puede.”

name: Nicole Cardoza
bio: Nicole Cardoza is an entrepreneur, author and speaker. She founded Anti-Racism Daily, a newsletter about taking action against racism, and Reclamation Ventures, which supports work on wellness and equity.

name: Brittany Packnett Cunningham
bio: Brittany Packnett Cunningham is an activist and former teacher. She led Teach For America in St. Louis, served on President Obama's Task Force on 21st Century Policing, and co-founded Campaign Zero, which works to end police violence.
clues: I was a teacher, then led Teach For America in St. Louis.
After the 2014 protests in Ferguson, Missouri, I served on President Obama's task force on policing.
I co-founded Campaign Zero, which works to end police violence.

name: Rachel Cargle
bio: Rachel Cargle is an American activist, author and public speaker who teaches about race and feminism. She founded The Loveland Foundation, which helps Black women and girls get access to therapy.

name: Ceyenne Doroshow
bio: Ceyenne Doroshow is an author and activist who founded G.L.I.T.S., an organization that provides housing and health care for Black transgender people. GQ called her a “Godmother” of the Black Trans Lives Matter movement.

name: Cathy Park Hong
bio: Cathy Park Hong is a Korean American poet and writer who has published three books of poetry. Her essay collection Minor Feelings, about Asian American identity, helped earn her a place on Time's 2021 list of the 100 most influential people.
clues: I've published three books of poetry that often mix languages together.
In 2020 I published an essay collection called Minor Feelings.
Time named me one of its 100 most influential people in 2021 for my writing about Asian American women.

name: Jonny Sun
bio: Jonny Sun is a Canadian author and illustrator. He wrote and drew the illustrated novel everyone's a aliebn when ur a aliebn too and the essay collection Goodbye, Again, and he has written for the TV shows BoJack Horseman and Mrs. Davis.
clues: I studied urban planning at MIT.
I've written for the animated TV show BoJack Horseman.
My illustrated book is about a little alien who lands on Earth and makes friends with the animals.

name: Amanda Gorman
bio: Amanda Gorman is a poet and the first person named National Youth Poet Laureate. In 2021, at age 22, she read her poem “The Hill We Climb” at President Biden's inauguration.
clues: I published my first book of poetry when I was 17.
As a child I worked hard to overcome a speech difference.
I was the first National Youth Poet Laureate.
I read my poem “The Hill We Climb” at a presidential inauguration.

name: Mimi Zhu
bio: Mimi Zhu is a queer Chinese-Australian writer and artist based in Brooklyn, New York. Their writing and art have appeared in The New York Times and The Guardian, among others.

name: Darien Sutton
bio: Dr. Darien Sutton is a board-certified emergency medicine doctor and a medical correspondent for ABC News. He trained at Bellevue Hospital in New York, where he became committed to fixing unfair differences in health care.

name: Bayard Rustin
bio: Bayard Rustin was a civil rights leader and the main organizer of the 1963 March on Washington, where Martin Luther King Jr. gave his “I Have a Dream” speech. He was openly gay at a time when that was dangerous, and he championed nonviolence and gay rights.
clues: I was raised as a Quaker and believed deeply in nonviolent protest.
I advised Martin Luther King Jr. on Gandhi's methods of nonviolence.
In 2013 I was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, years after my death.
I was the chief organizer of the 1963 March on Washington.

name: Laverne Cox
bio: Laverne Cox is an actress and advocate. Her role on Orange Is the New Black made her the first openly transgender person nominated for a Primetime Emmy in an acting category. She works to raise awareness of transgender people's lives.
clues: I studied dance and acting in New York City.
In 2014 I was the first openly transgender person on the cover of Time magazine.
I was the first openly transgender person nominated for a Primetime Emmy for acting.
I played Sophia Burset on Orange Is the New Black.

name: Mindy Kaling
bio: Mindy Kaling is an actress, comedian, writer and producer. She wrote for and acted in The Office, then created The Mindy Project and co-created Never Have I Ever. She received the National Medal of Arts in 2021.
clues: I was one of the youngest writers on The Office, and I also played Kelly Kapoor.
I created the TV show The Mindy Project.
My parents immigrated from India, and my real last name is Chokalingam.

name: Kehinde Wiley
bio: Kehinde Wiley is a portrait painter known for bold, colorful paintings of Black people posed like the subjects of famous European paintings. In 2017 he was chosen to paint President Barack Obama's official portrait for the National Portrait Gallery.
clues: I grew up in Los Angeles and earned a master's degree in art from Yale.
I paint everyday Black people in the poses of kings and nobles from old European paintings.
I painted Barack Obama's official presidential portrait.

name: Kim Petras
bio: Kim Petras is a German pop singer and songwriter based in Los Angeles. In 2023 she and Sam Smith won a Grammy for “Unholy,” making her the first transgender woman to win in the Best Pop Duo/Group Performance category.
review: Some of her music has explicit lyrics. Teachers may want to decide whether to include her.

name: Alice Ball
bio: Alice Ball was a chemist who developed the first effective treatment for Hansen's disease (leprosy), known as the “Ball method.” She was the first woman and the first African American to earn a master's degree from the College of Hawaii. She died at just 24, and for years another scientist took credit for her work.
clues: I was born in Seattle, and my father was a photographer.
I was the first woman to earn a master's degree from the College of Hawaii.
After I died, another scientist published my discovery under his own name.
My “Ball method” was the first effective treatment for leprosy.

name: Ai-jen Poo
bio: Ai-jen Poo is a labor activist and president of the National Domestic Workers Alliance, which fights for fair pay and protections for nannies, housekeepers and caregivers. She also leads Caring Across Generations, a coalition working to improve care for older people and people with disabilities.
clues: I won a MacArthur “genius” grant in 2014.
I lead a coalition working to improve care for older people and people with disabilities.
I'm president of the National Domestic Workers Alliance.

name: Ajay Bhatt
bio: Ajay Bhatt is an Indian American computer architect who helped create USB, the connector that links phones, keyboards and other devices to computers. He worked on many widely used computer technologies at Intel.
clues: I grew up in India and moved to the United States for graduate school.
I spent most of my career designing computer technology at Intel.
I helped invent the USB connector.

name: Yuri Kochiyama
bio: Yuri Kochiyama was a Japanese American civil rights activist. During World War II she and her family were forced into an incarceration camp in Arkansas, which shaped her lifelong fight against racism. In Harlem she worked alongside Malcolm X and later supported many movements for justice.
clues: I grew up in San Pedro, California, the daughter of Japanese immigrants.
During World War II, my family was forced into an incarceration camp in Arkansas.
In Harlem, I became friends with Malcolm X.

name: Eric Yuan
bio: Eric Yuan is a Chinese American engineer and businessman who founded Zoom, the video-calling company. He moved to the United States after his visa application was turned down eight times.
clues: I was turned down for a U.S. visa eight times before I was finally approved.
I worked as an engineer at the video company Webex.
I founded the video-calling company Zoom.

name: Sudha Chandran
bio: Sudha Chandran is an Indian actress and Bharatanatyam dancer. After losing part of her leg in a car accident, she learned to dance with a prosthetic leg and returned to the stage. She played herself in the 1985 film Mayuri, which told her story.
clues: I began studying classical Indian dance when I was a small child.
After a car accident, part of my right leg had to be amputated.
With a prosthetic “Jaipur foot,” I returned to dancing Bharatanatyam.
I played myself in the film Mayuri, about my own life.

name: David Blunkett
bio: David Blunkett is a British politician who has been blind since birth. He served as Secretary of State for Education and Employment and later as Home Secretary, and he now sits in the House of Lords.
clues: I was born blind and went to schools for blind children.
I was a member of Parliament for Sheffield for 28 years.
I was in charge of Britain's schools as Secretary of State for Education.

name: Frida Kahlo
bio: Frida Kahlo was a Mexican painter known for her self-portraits and images drawn from Mexican culture. She painted through chronic pain after polio and a serious bus accident.
clues: I planned to become a doctor until a bus accident when I was 18 changed my path.
I painted many works lying in bed, with a mirror mounted above me.
I married the famous muralist Diego Rivera twice.
I'm known for my self-portraits and for my Blue House in Mexico City.

name: Ryan O'Connell
bio: Ryan O'Connell is a writer and actor who has cerebral palsy. He turned his memoir I'm Special into the Netflix series Special, which he wrote and starred in, telling stories about being gay and disabled.

name: Josephine Baker
bio: Josephine Baker was an American-born French dancer, singer and actress. During World War II she spied for the French Resistance. She refused to perform for segregated audiences and spoke at the 1963 March on Washington.
clues: I grew up poor in St. Louis and moved to Paris as a young dancer.
During World War II, I carried secret messages for the French Resistance.
I adopted 12 children from around the world and called them my “Rainbow Tribe.”
In 2021 I became the first Black woman honored in France's Panthéon.

name: Michael Dillon
bio: Michael Dillon was a British doctor and writer, and one of the first known transgender men to receive gender-affirming medical care. He wrote one of the first books about being transgender and later became a Buddhist monk.

name: Ifti Nasim
bio: Ifti Nasim was a Pakistani American poet who moved to the United States to escape persecution for being gay. His book Narman was the first openly gay poetry collection in the Urdu language, and he founded Sangat to support LGBTQ+ South Asian youth in Chicago.

name: Simon Nkoli
bio: Simon Nkoli was a South African activist who fought apartheid and fought for gay rights and people living with HIV. He organized South Africa's first Pride march, and his work helped make South Africa's constitution protect people from discrimination based on sexual orientation.
clues: I was put on trial for treason for protesting apartheid.
I organized South Africa's first Pride march in 1990.
I was one of the first Black South Africans to speak openly about living with HIV.

name: Nancy Cárdenas
bio: Nancy Cárdenas was a Mexican actress, poet, writer and feminist. In 1973 she became the first person to speak openly on Mexican television about being a lesbian, and she helped organize Mexico City's first gay pride marches.

name: Abraham Nemeth
bio: Abraham Nemeth was a blind mathematician and professor. He created Nemeth Braille, a code that lets blind people read and write math, and it is still used today.
clues: I was born blind in New York City.
I taught math at the University of Detroit.
I invented a braille code for writing math, and it's named after me.

name: Wanda Díaz-Merced
bio: Wanda Díaz-Merced is a Puerto Rican astronomer who lost her sight as a young scientist. She uses sonification, turning data into sound, so she and others can study space by listening. The BBC named her one of seven trailblazing women in science.
clues: I grew up in Puerto Rico and dreamed of studying the stars.
As a student, I gradually lost my eyesight.
I turn data from space into sound so I can study it by listening.

name: Richard Mankin
bio: Richard Mankin is a research entomologist (insect scientist) with the U.S. Department of Agriculture. He listens to insects, using sound-detecting tools to find hidden pests in crops and trees. He has a physical disability and has worked to show that disability is no barrier to a career in science.

name: Bernard Morin
bio: Bernard Morin was a French mathematician who was blind from age six. He studied the shapes of surfaces and worked out how a sphere could, in theory, be turned inside out, a famous geometry puzzle, by picturing the shapes in his mind.
clues: I lost my sight to glaucoma when I was six years old.
I'm a topologist, a mathematician who studies shapes and surfaces.
I figured out how a sphere could be turned inside out without tearing, and a surface is named after me.

name: Nyle DiMarco
bio: Nyle DiMarco is a Deaf model, actor and activist. He was the first Deaf winner of America's Next Top Model and also won Dancing with the Stars. He works to make sure Deaf children have access to sign language.
clues: I was born into a large Deaf family.
I was the first Deaf winner of America's Next Top Model.
I won Dancing with the Stars, dancing to music I couldn't hear.

name: Caroline Solomon
bio: Dr. Caroline Solomon is a Deaf biology professor at Gallaudet University, a university for Deaf and hard-of-hearing students in Washington, D.C. She helped create a collection of American Sign Language signs for science terms, and NPR named her one of its 50 great teachers.

name: Marie Maynard Daly
bio: Marie Maynard Daly was a biochemist and the first African American woman in the U.S. to earn a Ph.D. in chemistry. Her research on cholesterol and blood pressure helped explain how heart disease develops.
clues: I earned my Ph.D. from Columbia University in 1947.
I studied how cholesterol and blood pressure affect the heart.
I was the first African American woman in the U.S. to earn a Ph.D. in chemistry.

name: Temple Grandin
bio: Temple Grandin is an autistic professor of animal science. She redesigned livestock handling to be more humane and has become one of the best-known voices on autism.
clues: I didn't speak until I was almost four years old.
As a young woman I built a “squeeze machine” to help calm my nerves.
I've designed animal handling systems used for a large share of the cattle in North America.
I'm a professor of animal science and one of the best-known autistic people in the world.

name: Rosa May Billinghurst
bio: Rosa May Billinghurst was a British suffragette who fought for women's right to vote. Polio affected her legs as a child, so she campaigned from a hand-powered tricycle, and she was arrested several times for protesting.
clues: Polio affected my legs when I was a small child.
I rode a hand-powered tricycle to protests and marches.
I was jailed for fighting for women's right to vote in Britain.

name: Farida Bedwei
bio: Farida Bedwei is a Ghanaian software engineer who has cerebral palsy. She co-founded Logiciel, a financial technology company, and builds banking software used across Ghana.

name: Mahlia Amatina
bio: Mahlia Amatina is a British abstract artist on the autism spectrum. Her colorful paintings share what her sensory experiences feel like, and she was named one of the Top 50 Influential Neurodivergent Women in 2019.
review: Photo file was named matima.jpg and wasn't linked to anyone; it appears to be her, but please confirm.

name: Florence Welch
bio: Florence Welch is an English singer and the lead singer and songwriter of the band Florence and the Machine. She has spoken openly about having dyslexia and dyspraxia.

name: Ursula Burns
bio: Ursula Burns grew up in public housing in New York City, studied mechanical engineering, and started at Xerox as a summer intern. In 2009 she became Xerox's CEO, the first Black woman to lead a Fortune 500 company.
clues: I grew up in a public housing project in New York City.
I studied mechanical engineering and started at my company as a summer intern.
I was the first Black woman to lead a Fortune 500 company.

name: Maya Lin
bio: Maya Lin is an American architect and artist. As a 21-year-old student at Yale, she won the contest to design the Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Washington, D.C. She also designed the Civil Rights Memorial in Montgomery, Alabama.
clues: My parents immigrated from China, and I grew up in Athens, Ohio.
I designed the Civil Rights Memorial in Montgomery, Alabama.
As a college student, I won a contest to design the Vietnam Veterans Memorial.

name: John Nash
bio: John Nash was an American mathematician whose work on game theory changed economics. He lived with schizophrenia for many years and returned to his research, winning the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 1994. The film A Beautiful Mind is based on his life.
clues: I wrote a famous, very short thesis on game theory when I was 21.
I lived with schizophrenia for many years before returning to my work.
The movie A Beautiful Mind is about my life.

name: Mae Jemison
bio: Mae Jemison is an engineer, doctor and former NASA astronaut. In 1992 she flew on the Space Shuttle Endeavour, becoming the first African American woman in space.
clues: I worked as a Peace Corps doctor in Sierra Leone and Liberia.
I studied chemical engineering and African American studies at Stanford.
In 1992 I became the first African American woman to travel into space.

name: Sylvia Rivera
bio: Sylvia Rivera was a Latina gay liberation and transgender rights activist in New York City. With her friend Marsha P. Johnson, she co-founded STAR, which gave shelter to homeless LGBTQ+ young people.
clues: I left home at 11 and lived on the streets of New York City.
I fought for transgender people to be included in gay rights laws.
With Marsha P. Johnson, I co-founded STAR to house homeless queer and trans youth.

name: Marsha P. Johnson
bio: Marsha P. Johnson was a gay liberation activist and a prominent figure of the 1969 Stonewall uprising. She co-founded STAR to support homeless LGBTQ+ youth in New York City.
clues: I said the “P” in my name stood for “Pay It No Mind.”
I was known for wearing crowns of flowers.
With my friend Sylvia Rivera, I co-founded STAR to house homeless queer and trans youth.
I was part of the 1969 Stonewall uprising in New York City.

name: Ellen Ochoa
bio: In 1993 Ellen Ochoa became the first Latina to go to space. She later served as director of NASA's Johnson Space Center.
clues: I'm a classically trained flutist, and I once played my flute in a place no one had played before.
As an engineer, I helped invent optical systems for analyzing images and hold patents for them.
I flew on four space shuttle missions, then later ran NASA's Johnson Space Center.
In 1993 I became the first Latina to go to space.

name: Chien-Shiung Wu
bio: Chien-Shiung Wu was a Chinese American physicist. Her famous 1956 experiment showed that a basic law of physics, the conservation of parity, does not always hold.
clues: I left China in 1936 to study physics in California.
During World War II I worked on the Manhattan Project.
My 1956 experiment proved that a “law” of physics called parity isn't always true. Two male colleagues won the Nobel Prize for the idea.
People called me the “First Lady of Physics.”

name: Wilma Mankiller
roles: Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation
bio: Wilma Mankiller was the first woman elected Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation. She focused on community development, health care and education.
clues: When I was 11, a federal relocation program moved my family from Oklahoma to San Francisco.
The 1969 occupation of Alcatraz Island inspired me to become an activist.
I helped a small rural community in Oklahoma build its own water system.
In 1987 I became the first woman elected Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation.

name: Mary Jackson
bio: Mary Jackson started as a “human computer” in NASA's segregated West Area Computing unit and, in 1958, became NASA's first Black female engineer. Later she worked to help more women get hired and promoted in science and engineering jobs at NASA.

photo.commons: Mary Jackson with a model (medium close-up).jpg

clues: I started my NASA career as a “human computer” in a segregated office.
I took engineering classes so I could be promoted.
In 1958 I became NASA's first Black female engineer.

name: Dorothy Vaughan
bio: Dorothy Vaughan was a mathematician and teacher who became the first African American woman to supervise a group of staff at NASA's Langley center. When electronic computers arrived, she taught herself and her team the programming language Fortran so they wouldn't be left behind.
clues: I was a schoolteacher before I worked on airplane and rocket math.
In 1949 I became the first African American woman to supervise a team at my research center.
When computers arrived at NASA, I taught myself and my team the Fortran programming language.

name: Gladys West
bio: Gladys West was a mathematician whose models of the exact shape of the Earth became part of the Global Positioning System (GPS). She was inducted into the U.S. Air Force Hall of Fame in 2018.
clues: I was inducted into the U.S. Air Force Hall of Fame in 2018.
I made mathematical models of the exact shape of the Earth.
My work helped make GPS, the system that tells your phone where you are, possible.

name: George Washington Carver
bio: George Washington Carver was one of the most prominent Black scientists of the early 1900s. As a professor at Tuskegee Institute, he taught poor farmers how to restore soil worn out by cotton by growing crops like peanuts and sweet potatoes.
clues: I wrote practical guides for poor farmers, some with recipes in them.
I was a professor at Tuskegee Institute in Alabama.
I'm famous for promoting peanuts and sweet potatoes to help restore worn-out soil.

name: Charles R. Drew
bio: Charles Drew was a surgeon who developed better ways to store blood and helped set up large blood banks early in World War II, saving thousands of lives. He protested the Red Cross policy of separating blood donations by race, which had no scientific basis.
clues: I resigned from the American Red Cross to protest its policy of separating blood by race.
During World War II, I helped create large-scale blood banks.
I developed better ways to store blood for transfusions.

name: Neil deGrasse Tyson
bio: Neil deGrasse Tyson is an astrophysicist, author and science communicator. Since 1996 he has directed the Hayden Planetarium at the American Museum of Natural History in New York City, and he is known for explaining space science to the public on TV and in books.
clues: I wrote a monthly column called “Universe” for Natural History magazine.
I founded the Department of Astrophysics at the American Museum of Natural History.
I've directed the Hayden Planetarium in New York City since 1996.

name: Rosalind Franklin
bio: Rosalind Franklin was an English chemist whose X-ray images were central to discovering the structure of DNA. Her contribution was largely unrecognized during her life, and she died at 37, before the Nobel Prize was awarded for the discovery.
clues: I studied the structures of coal, graphite and viruses.
I used X-rays to take pictures of the shapes of molecules.
My work was central to discovering the structure of DNA, but I got little credit while I was alive.

name: Marie Curie
bio: Marie Curie was a Polish-born physicist and chemist who did pioneering research on radioactivity in France. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, and she is still the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.
clues: I was born in Warsaw and studied at a secret university.
I discovered the elements polonium and radium.
I was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, and I won a second one in a different science.

name: Grace Hopper
bio: Grace Hopper was a computer scientist, mathematician and U.S. Navy rear admiral. She was one of the first programmers of the Harvard Mark I computer, and her ideas led to programming languages that use words instead of numbers, including COBOL, which is still used today.
clues: I earned a Ph.D. in math from Yale and taught at Vassar College.
I joined the U.S. Navy during World War II and rose to rear admiral.
My ideas led to programming languages written in words, like COBOL.

name: Hedy Lamarr
bio: Hedy Lamarr was an Austrian-born Hollywood film star who was also an inventor. During World War II she co-invented a radio guidance system with composer George Antheil, an idea that helped lead to later wireless technologies.

photo.commons: Hedy Lamarr Publicity Photo for The Heavenly Body 1944.jpg

clues: I was born in Austria and secretly fled to Paris.
I became a Hollywood film star in the 1930s and 1940s.
During World War II, I co-invented a radio guidance system with a composer.

name: Jane Goodall
bio: Jane Goodall was an English scientist who studied wild chimpanzees in Tanzania for more than 60 years. Her research showed that chimpanzees use tools, have complex emotions and form lasting bonds, changing how people think about the line between humans and other animals.

photo.commons: Deputy Secretary Higginbottom Poses for a Photo With Dr. Jane Goodall and the State Department's Global Health Diplomacy Director Jordan in Washington (22365513310) (2) (cropped 2).jpg

clues: I began my research in 1960 with help from the scientist Louis Leakey.
I studied animals at Gombe Stream National Park in Tanzania.
I'm the world's best-known expert on wild chimpanzees.

name: Rachel Carson
bio: Rachel Carson was a marine biologist and writer whose books about the ocean became bestsellers. Her 1962 book Silent Spring warned about the dangers of chemical pesticides and helped start the modern environmental movement.
clues: I started my career as a biologist for the U.S. Bureau of Fisheries.
My book The Sea Around Us won a National Book Award.
My 1962 book Silent Spring warned about the dangers of pesticides.

name: Sally Ride
bio: Sally Ride was an astronaut and physicist who in 1983 became the first American woman in space. At 32 she was also the youngest American astronaut to fly. She later worked to get girls interested in science.
clues: I earned degrees in both physics and English literature from Stanford.
I helped develop the Space Shuttle's robotic arm.
In 1983 I became the first American woman in space.

name: Tu Youyou
bio: Tu Youyou is a Chinese chemist who discovered artemisinin, a medicine for malaria that has saved millions of lives. In 2015 she became the first Chinese woman to win a Nobel Prize in a science category.
clues: I was born, educated and did all of my research in China.
I discovered artemisinin, a medicine that treats malaria.
In 2015 I became the first Chinese Nobel Prize winner in Physiology or Medicine.

name: Kalpana Chawla
bio: Kalpana Chawla was an Indian-born American astronaut and aerospace engineer, and the first woman of Indian heritage to go to space. She died with her six crewmates when the Space Shuttle Columbia broke apart in 2003.

photo.commons: Kalpana Chawla, NASA photo portrait in orange suit.jpg

clues: I decided I wanted to be an aerospace engineer when I was 12.
I grew up in Karnal, India.
I was the first woman of Indian heritage to fly into space.

name: Patricia Bath
bio: Patricia Bath was an eye doctor who invented new ways to perform cataract surgery and championed eye care for communities that had little access to it. She was the first African American woman doctor to receive a patent for a medical invention.
clues: As a high school student, I won a scholarship to study cancer research.
I was the first woman to lead an eye surgery training program in the U.S.
I was the first African American woman doctor to patent a medical invention.

name: Kizzmekia Corbett-Helaire
bio: Kizzmekia Corbett-Helaire is a viral immunologist who was a key scientist on the National Institutes of Health team that worked on a COVID-19 vaccine. She is now a professor at Harvard.
clues: I earned my Ph.D. in microbiology and immunology at the University of North Carolina.
I'm a professor at Harvard's School of Public Health.
I was a key scientist on the government team that worked on a COVID-19 vaccine.

name: Gitanjali Rao
bio: Gitanjali Rao is an American inventor and STEM advocate who won the Discovery Education 3M Young Scientist Challenge in 2017. In 2020 Time named her its first-ever “Kid of the Year,” and she runs innovation workshops for students around the world.
clues: I run innovation workshops for students around the world.
I won the 3M Young Scientist Challenge when I was a kid.
In 2020 Time magazine named me its first-ever “Kid of the Year.”

name: Mario Molina
bio: Mario Molina was a Mexican chemist who helped discover that chemicals called CFCs were destroying Earth's ozone layer. He shared the 1995 Nobel Prize in Chemistry and was the first Mexican-born scientist to win it.
clues: I taught at MIT and the University of California.
I helped discover the hole in the ozone layer over Antarctica.
I was the first Mexican-born scientist to win the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

name: Franklin Chang-Díaz
bio: Franklin Chang-Díaz is a Costa Rican-born American engineer, physicist and former NASA astronaut. He flew on seven Space Shuttle missions, tying the record, and was the first Latin American immigrant chosen as a NASA astronaut.
clues: I founded a rocket company called Ad Astra.
I became a U.S. citizen in 1977.
I flew seven Space Shuttle missions and was born in Costa Rica.

name: Ynés Mexía

clues: I also competed as a pairs skater with Rudy Galindo.
I was World champion in 1991 and 1992.
In 1992 I became the first Asian American to win Winter Olympic gold.

name: Naomi Osaka
bio: Naomi Osaka is a Japanese tennis player with a Haitian American father and a Japanese mother. She was the first Asian player ranked No. 1 in singles and has won four major titles.
clues: I was born in Japan and have trained in the U.S. since I was three.
My father is Haitian American and my mother is Japanese.
I was the first Asian player ranked world No. 1 in tennis singles.

name: Quinn
bio: Quinn is a Canadian soccer player. At the Tokyo Olympics, Quinn became the first openly nonbinary transgender athlete to compete at the Olympics and to win a gold medal.
clues: I was the first Canadian to play women's college soccer at Duke University.
I play midfield for Canada's national team.
At the Tokyo Olympics, I was the first openly nonbinary transgender athlete to win gold.

name: Megan Rapinoe
bio: Megan Rapinoe is a former U.S. soccer star who won two FIFA Women's World Cups and an Olympic gold medal. In 2019 she won the Ballon d'Or Féminin and was named the best women's player in the world.
clues: I co-captained the U.S. women's national team.
I won the Ballon d'Or Féminin in 2019.
I won the Women's World Cup with the U.S. in 2015 and 2019.

name: Mohamed Salah
bio: Mohamed Salah is an Egyptian soccer player and captain of Egypt's national team, nicknamed the “Egyptian King.” He is the all-time top foreign goalscorer in England's Premier League.

photo.commons: Mohamed Salah Argentina v Egypt 7 July 2026-163 (cropped).jpg

clues: I started my career with a club in Egypt and then played in Switzerland and Italy.
I captain Egypt's national team.
I'm called the “Egyptian King” and I'm the top foreign scorer in Premier League history.

name: Ibtihaj Muhammad
bio: Ibtihaj Muhammad is an Olympic fencer and author. At the 2016 Olympics she became the first American woman to compete in hijab and the first American Muslim woman to win an Olympic medal.

photo.commons: Ibtihaj Muhammad podium 2013 Fencing WCH SFS-EQ t215413.jpg

clues: I've written a New York Times bestselling book.
I won a bronze medal in team sabre at the 2016 Olympics.
I was the first American woman to compete at the Olympics in hijab.

name: Kathrine Switzer
bio: Kathrine Switzer is a marathon runner who in 1967 became the first woman to run the Boston Marathon as an officially registered runner. A race official tried to pull her off the course, but she finished.

photo.commons: Kathrine Switzer at the 2011 Berlin Marathon Expo.jpg

clues: I signed up for a race using only my initials, “K.V.”
A race official tried to pull me off the course, but I finished anyway.
In 1967 I was the first woman to officially run the Boston Marathon.

name: Pelé
bio: Pelé was a Brazilian soccer player and one of the greatest players in history. He was named Athlete of the Century by the International Olympic Committee in 1999.
clues: My real name was Edson Arantes do Nascimento.
I scored more than 1,000 goals in my career.
I'm a Brazilian soccer legend known by a single name.

name: Jim Abbott
bio: Jim Abbott is a former Major League Baseball pitcher who was born without a right hand. He won an Olympic gold medal in 1988 and pitched for 10 seasons in the major leagues.
clues: I grew up in Flint, Michigan.
I won a gold medal with the U.S. baseball team at the 1988 Olympics.
I pitched in the major leagues even though I was born without a right hand.

name: Grandma Moses
bio: Anna Mary Robertson Moses, known as Grandma Moses, was a folk artist who began painting seriously at age 78. She became famous in her 80s and 90s and appeared on the cover of Time magazine in 1953.
clues: I worked as a live-in housekeeper starting at age 12.
Arthritis pushed me to focus on painting instead of embroidery.
I started painting seriously at 78 and became famous as “Grandma.”

name: Laura Ingalls Wilder
bio: Laura Ingalls Wilder was a teacher and writer who published the first of her Little House books at age 65. The series is based on her childhood in a pioneer family.
clues: I worked as a teacher and a journalist.
I published my first famous book when I was 65.
I wrote the Little House on the Prairie books about my own childhood.

name: Thurgood Marshall
bio: Thurgood Marshall was a civil rights lawyer who won the landmark 1954 case Brown v. Board of Education, which ruled school segregation unconstitutional. In 1967 he became the first African American justice on the U.S. Supreme Court.
clues: I won 29 of the 32 civil rights cases I argued before the Supreme Court.
I led the NAACP Legal Defense Fund.
I won Brown v. Board of Education and became the first Black Supreme Court justice.

name: Sonia Sotomayor
bio: Sonia Sotomayor grew up in the Bronx, the daughter of Puerto Rican-born parents. After graduating from Princeton and Yale Law School, she became a prosecutor and judge, and in 2009 she became the first Latina justice on the U.S. Supreme Court.
clues: I grew up in the Bronx, and my mother raised me after my father died when I was nine.
I worked as an assistant district attorney in New York.
In 2009 I became the first Latina justice on the U.S. Supreme Court.

name: Ruth Bader Ginsburg
bio: Ruth Bader Ginsburg was a lawyer who fought for gender equality and served on the U.S. Supreme Court from 1993 until 2020. She was the first Jewish woman and the second woman to serve on the Court.

photo.commons: Ruth Bader Ginsburg official SCOTUS portrait (cropped).jpg

clues: Before becoming a judge, I argued cases about equal rights for women.
I was the second woman to serve on the U.S. Supreme Court.
People called me “RBG.”

name: Ketanji Brown Jackson
bio: Ketanji Brown Jackson was raised in Miami and studied at Harvard. She was a federal public defender and judge before becoming the first Black woman on the U.S. Supreme Court in 2022.
clues: I clerked for Justice Stephen Breyer, whose seat I later took.
I'm the first former federal public defender on the Supreme Court.
In 2022 I became the first Black woman on the U.S. Supreme Court.

name: Constance Baker Motley
bio: Constance Baker Motley was a civil rights lawyer who helped Thurgood Marshall on Brown v. Board of Education. She was the first Black woman to argue before the U.S. Supreme Court, winning nine of her ten cases there, and later became a federal judge.

photo.commons: Mrs. Constance B. Motley, first woman Senator, 21st Senatorial District, N.Y., raising hand in V sign.jpg

clues: I was a New York state senator and Manhattan Borough President.
I helped Thurgood Marshall on Brown v. Board of Education.
I was the first Black woman to argue a case before the U.S. Supreme Court.

name: Pauli Murray
bio: Pauli Murray was a civil rights activist, legal scholar and author whose ideas shaped the fight against both race and sex discrimination. Murray was arrested in 1940 for refusing to move to the back of a bus in Virginia and later became an Episcopal priest.
clues: I moved to New York at 16 to attend Hunter College.
In 1940 I was arrested for sitting in the whites-only section of a Virginia bus.
My legal ideas helped win protections against sex discrimination, and I later became an Episcopal priest.

name: Fred Korematsu
bio: Fred Korematsu was a Japanese American who refused to go to an incarceration camp during World War II. He lost his case at the Supreme Court in 1944, but his conviction was overturned four decades later.
clues: I challenged a presidential order during World War II.
My Supreme Court case in 1944 is named after me.
I refused to report to a camp for Japanese Americans, and my conviction was overturned 40 years later.

name: Shirley Chisholm
bio: Shirley Chisholm was the first Black woman elected to the U.S. Congress, in 1968. In 1972 she became the first Black candidate to run for a major party's presidential nomination.
clues: I spent part of my childhood in Barbados.
I represented Brooklyn in Congress for seven terms.
In 1968 I became the first Black woman elected to Congress.

name: Patsy Mink
bio: Patsy Mink was a Japanese American lawyer from Maui and the first woman of color elected to the U.S. Congress. She is known for her work on laws advancing women's rights and education, including Title IX.
clues: I grew up on the island of Maui and was my high school's valedictorian.
I served in Congress for 24 years.
I was the first woman of color elected to Congress.

name: Barbara Jordan
bio: Barbara Jordan was the first African American elected to the Texas Senate since Reconstruction and one of the first Black members of Congress from the South since 1901. She was famous for her powerful speeches.
clues: I was the first African American in the Texas Senate since Reconstruction.
I became famous for a speech during the Nixon impeachment hearings.
I was the first Black woman to give the keynote at a Democratic National Convention.

name: Harvey Milk
bio: Harvey Milk was the first openly gay man elected to public office in California, on San Francisco's Board of Supervisors. He was a powerful voice for gay rights before he was assassinated in 1978.

photo.commons: Harvey Milk in front of camera shop November 1977 (cropped).jpg

clues: I opened a camera store in San Francisco.
I ran for city supervisor more than once before I won.
I was the first openly gay man elected to public office in California.

name: Dalip Singh Saund
bio: Dalip Singh Saund was an Indian-born American farmer and politician. In 1956 he became the first Asian American, the first Sikh and the first Indian American elected to the U.S. Congress.
clues: I came to the U.S. in 1920 to study at the University of California.
I was a farmer in California's Imperial Valley.
I was the first Asian American and first Sikh elected to Congress.

name: Deb Haaland
bio: Deb Haaland is an enrolled member of the Laguna Pueblo. She was one of the first two Native American women elected to Congress and served as U.S. Secretary of the Interior from 2021 to 2025, the first Native American cabinet secretary.
clues: I'm an enrolled member of the Laguna Pueblo in New Mexico.
I was one of the first two Native American women elected to Congress.
I was the first Native American to serve in a president's cabinet.

name: Tammy Duckworth
bio: Tammy Duckworth was born in Bangkok, Thailand, and raised in Hawaii. As an Army helicopter pilot in Iraq, she lost both legs when her helicopter was hit. She went on to serve in Congress and represents Illinois in the U.S. Senate.
clues: I was born in Bangkok and grew up in Honolulu.
I flew Black Hawk helicopters in the U.S. Army.
I lost both legs in the Iraq War and was later elected to the U.S. Senate.

name: Barack Obama
bio: Barack Obama was born in Honolulu and worked as a community organizer and civil rights lawyer. He served as the 44th president of the United States from 2009 to 2017, the first African American president.
clues: I was the first Black president of the Harvard Law Review.
I worked as a community organizer in Chicago.
I was the 44th president of the United States.

name: Kamala Harris
roles: Vice President of the United States
bio: Kamala Harris, the daughter of Indian and Jamaican immigrants, was a prosecutor and attorney general of California before serving in the U.S. Senate. As vice president from 2021 to 2025 she was the first woman, first African American and first Asian American to hold the office.
clues: I graduated from Howard University.
I was attorney general of California.
I was the first woman to serve as vice president of the United States.

name: Haben Girma
bio: Haben Girma is a disability rights advocate and the first deafblind graduate of Harvard Law School. She works to make technology and education accessible to people with disabilities.
clues: My family came from Eritrea.
I'm a disability rights lawyer and speaker.
I was the first deafblind person to graduate from Harvard Law School.

name: Daniel Inouye
bio: Daniel Inouye was a Japanese American soldier who lost his right arm fighting in World War II with the 442nd Infantry Regiment. He represented Hawaii in the U.S. Senate for nearly 50 years.
clues: I planned to become a doctor before World War II.
I lost my right arm fighting with the 442nd Infantry Regiment.
I represented Hawaii in the U.S. Senate from 1963 until 2012.

name: Harriet Tubman
bio: Harriet Tubman escaped slavery and then made about 13 trips back to lead some 70 enslaved people to freedom on the Underground Railroad. During the Civil War she served as a scout and spy for the Union Army. A head injury in her youth caused lifelong dizziness and sleeping spells.
clues: A head injury when I was young gave me dizziness and sudden sleeping spells for life.
During the Civil War I was a scout and spy for the Union Army.
I led about 70 people to freedom on the Underground Railroad.

name: Frederick Douglass
bio: Frederick Douglass escaped slavery in Maryland in 1838 and became the most important African American civil rights leader of the 1800s. His powerful speeches and writing showed the world the truth about slavery.

photo.commons: Frederick Douglass as a younger man.jpg

clues: My birth name was Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey.
People found it hard to believe that such a great speaker had once been enslaved.
I escaped slavery in 1838 and became a famous abolitionist writer and speaker.

name: Sojourner Truth
bio: Sojourner Truth was born into slavery in New York and escaped with her baby daughter in 1826. She went to court to win back her son and became a powerful speaker for abolition and women's rights.
clues: I was the first Black woman to win a court case against a white man, to get my son back.
I chose my own name in 1843.
My 1851 speech became known as “Ain't I a Woman?”

name: Rosa Parks
bio: Rosa Parks was a civil rights activist and NAACP secretary in Montgomery, Alabama. Her 1955 refusal to give up her bus seat sparked the Montgomery bus boycott, and she is called the “mother of the civil rights movement.”

photo.commons: Rosa Parks being fingerprinted by Deputy Sheriff D.H. Lackey after being arrested on February 22, 1956, during the Montgomery bus boycott.jpg

clues: I was secretary of the NAACP chapter in Montgomery.
It took me three tries to register to vote.
In 1955 I refused to give up my seat on a Montgomery bus.

name: Martin Luther King Jr.
bio: Martin Luther King Jr. was a Baptist minister and a leader of the civil rights movement. He used nonviolent protest to fight segregation and led the Montgomery bus boycott and the March on Washington, where he gave his “I Have a Dream” speech.

photo.commons: The Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Color Portrait (high quality).jpg

clues: I was born Michael King Jr.
I was the first president of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference.
I gave the “I Have a Dream” speech.

name: Cesar Chavez
bio: Cesar Chavez was a Mexican American labor leader. With Dolores Huerta and Gilbert Padilla, he co-founded the National Farm Workers Association, which became the United Farm Workers and fought for better pay and conditions for farmworkers.
clues: I was born in Yuma, Arizona, and served two years in the U.S. Navy.
I helped farmworkers register to vote.
I co-founded the United Farm Workers with Dolores Huerta.

name: Larry Itliong
bio: Larry Itliong was a Filipino American labor organizer who started the 1965 Delano grape strike when Filipino farmworkers walked off the fields demanding fair pay. He is called one of the fathers of the West Coast labor movement.
clues: My nickname was “Seven Fingers.”
I organized farmworkers on the West Coast starting in the 1930s.
I led Filipino farmworkers in starting the 1965 Delano grape strike.

name: Ida B. Wells
bio: Ida B. Wells was an investigative journalist and educator who exposed the truth about lynching in the 1890s. She was one of the founders of the NAACP.

photo.commons: Mary Garrity - Ida B. Wells-Barnett - Google Art Project - restoration crop.jpg

clues: I was a teacher before I became a journalist.
I wrote pamphlets called Southern Horrors and The Red Record.
I was a founder of the NAACP and an investigative journalist.

name: Fannie Lou Hamer
bio: Fannie Lou Hamer was a voting rights activist from Mississippi who helped organize Freedom Summer. She spoke for the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party at the 1964 Democratic National Convention and co-founded the National Women's Political Caucus.
clues: I was known for singing hymns at protests.
I helped organize Mississippi's Freedom Summer in 1964.
I spoke at the 1964 Democratic Convention for the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party.

name: Claudette Colvin
bio: Claudette Colvin was arrested at age 15 in Montgomery, Alabama, in March 1955 for refusing to give up her bus seat, nine months before Rosa Parks. She was a plaintiff in Browder v. Gayle, the court case that ended bus segregation in the city.
clues: I testified in court in the case that ended bus segregation in Montgomery.
I later worked as a nurse aide in New York.
At 15, I refused to give up my bus seat nine months before Rosa Parks did.

name: Ruby Bridges
bio: In 1960, six-year-old Ruby Bridges became the first African American child to attend the formerly whites-only William Frantz Elementary School in New Orleans. Norman Rockwell painted her walking to school in The Problem We All Live With.
clues: Norman Rockwell made a famous painting of me.
I was escorted to school by federal marshals.
In 1960 I became the first Black student at William Frantz Elementary School in New Orleans.

name: Sylvia Mendez
bio: When Sylvia Mendez was turned away from a “whites-only” school in California, her family sued. The 1946 case Mendez v. Westminster ended school segregation in California, years before Brown v. Board of Education.
clues: I later became a nurse.
When I was 10, a California school refused to let me enroll.
My family's case, Mendez v. Westminster, ended school segregation in California.

name: John Lewis
bio: John Lewis was a civil rights leader who joined the Freedom Rides and chaired the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. He led the 1965 march across the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma and later served in Congress for over 30 years.
clues: I took part in the 1960 Nashville sit-ins and the Freedom Rides.
I represented Georgia in Congress from 1987 until 2020.
I led marchers across the Edmund Pettus Bridge on “Bloody Sunday.”

name: Mary McLeod Bethune
bio: Mary McLeod Bethune was an educator who started a school for Black students that became Bethune-Cookman University. She founded the National Council of Negro Women and was the first Black woman to lead a federal agency office.
clues: I founded the National Council of Negro Women in 1935.
President Franklin Roosevelt appointed me to lead an office of a federal agency.
The school I started became Bethune-Cookman University.

name: Nelson Mandela
bio: Nelson Mandela was a lawyer and anti-apartheid leader who spent 27 years in prison. In 1994 he became South Africa's first Black president, elected in the country's first fully democratic election.
clues: I was born into the Thembu royal family.
I studied law and worked as a lawyer in Johannesburg.
In 1994 I became South Africa's first Black president.

name: Malala Yousafzai
bio: Malala Yousafzai is a Pakistani activist for girls' education. She spoke out when the Taliban banned girls from school in her home region, and at 17 she became the youngest person ever to win the Nobel Peace Prize.
clues: My father is also an education activist.
I spoke out when girls were banned from school in Swat, Pakistan.
At 17, I became the youngest Nobel Prize winner ever.

name: Helen Keller
bio: Helen Keller lost her sight and hearing as a baby. With her teacher Anne Sullivan she learned to read and write, became the first deafblind person in the U.S. to earn a college degree, and wrote 14 books.
clues: I wrote 14 books and hundreds of speeches.
My teacher, Anne Sullivan, taught me language when I was seven.
I was the first deafblind person in the U.S. to earn a college degree.

name: Judith Heumann
bio: Judith Heumann was a disability rights activist known as the “Mother of the Disability Rights Movement.” A wheelchair user, she fought for laws protecting people with disabilities and later worked at the World Bank and the State Department.
clues: I worked on disability rights at the World Bank and the State Department.
I'm a wheelchair user who fought for laws protecting disabled people.
I'm called the “Mother of the Disability Rights Movement.”

name: Alice Wong
bio: Alice Wong was a disability rights activist and writer in San Francisco who founded the Disability Visibility Project to record disabled people's stories. She was a MacArthur Fellow and wrote the memoir Year of the Tiger.

photo.commons: Alice Wong (1974–2025) in the video 'Celebration – 42nd Annual Northern California Book Awards'.png

clues: I was appointed to the National Council on Disability in 2013.
I wrote a memoir called Year of the Tiger.
I founded the Disability Visibility Project to share disabled people's stories.

name: Jaime Escalante
bio: Jaime Escalante was a Bolivian American teacher who taught calculus at Garfield High School in East Los Angeles from 1974 to 1991, helping students many people had written off succeed. His story was told in the 1988 film Stand and Deliver.
clues: I was born in Bolivia.
I taught at Garfield High School in East Los Angeles.
The movie Stand and Deliver tells the story of my calculus classes.

name: Madam C. J. Walker
bio: Madam C. J. Walker, born Sarah Breedlove, built a business selling hair care products for Black women. Guinness World Records lists her as the first woman in America to become a self-made millionaire, and she gave generously to causes like the NAACP.

photo.commons: Madam C. J. Walker by Addison N. Scurlock.jpg

clues: My birth name was Sarah Breedlove.
I made hair care products for Black women.
I'm recognized as America's first female self-made millionaire.

name: Oprah Winfrey
bio: Oprah Winfrey was born into poverty in rural Mississippi and became a media leader and talk show host. The Oprah Winfrey Show ran for 25 years, and she became one of the most influential women in the world.
clues: I was born in rural Mississippi to a teenage mother.
My TV talk show was broadcast from Chicago for 25 years.
I hosted The Oprah Winfrey Show.

name: Indra Nooyi
bio: Indra Nooyi is an Indian-born American business executive who was chairman and CEO of PepsiCo from 2006 to 2018. She was regularly ranked among the most powerful women in the world.
clues: I was born in India and moved to the U.S. as an adult.
I serve on the boards of Amazon and the International Cricket Council.
I was the CEO of PepsiCo for 12 years.

name: Tim Cook
bio: Tim Cook joined Apple in 1998 and became its CEO in 2011, growing it into one of the most valuable companies in the world. He is the most prominent openly gay leader of a major U.S. company.

photo.commons: Tim Cook in New York City - 2026 (cropped).jpg

clues: I joined my company in 1998 to run its worldwide operations.
I took over as CEO when the company's co-founder stepped down because of illness.
I led Apple as CEO from 2011 to 2026.

name: Grace Lee Boggs
bio: Grace Lee Boggs was a Chinese American activist, author and philosopher in Detroit who worked in the civil rights, Black Power and Asian American movements. She wrote a new book at age 95.
clues: I worked alongside my husband James Boggs for civil rights in Detroit.
I was active in the Black Power and Asian American movements.
I was still writing books when I was 95.

name: Jovita Idar
bio: Jovita Idar was a Mexican American journalist and teacher from Laredo, Texas, who used her writing to fight for the rights of Mexican Americans. She led the League of Mexican Women, which offered free education to Mexican children.
clues: I started my career at my father's newspaper, La Crónica.
I was from Laredo, Texas.
I led La Liga Femenil Mexicanista, which gave free schooling to Mexican children.

name: Rigoberta Menchú
bio: Rigoberta Menchú is a K'iche' human rights activist from Guatemala who has worked for the rights of Indigenous peoples. She won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1992 and later founded Guatemala's first Indigenous political party.

photo.commons: 20240620 NP PRESIDENTE BERNARDO AREVALO Y KARIN HERRERA PARTICIPAN EN DIALOGO PREMIO NOBEL DE LA PAZ 054.jpg

clues: I ran for president of Guatemala twice.
I founded my country's first Indigenous political party.
I'm a K'iche' activist who won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1992.

name: Sequoyah
bio: Sequoyah was a Cherokee polymath. He created a writing system for the Cherokee language, completed in 1821, and within 25 years almost every Cherokee person could read and write.
clues: I was also known as George Gist.
Within 25 years of my invention, nearly all Cherokee people could read.
I created a writing system for the Cherokee language.

name: Elouise Cobell
bio: Elouise Cobell, also known as Yellow Bird Woman, was a Blackfeet elder, banker and rancher. She led a lawsuit against the U.S. government for mismanaging money owed to Native Americans, which ended in a $3.4 billion settlement that included a scholarship fund.
clues: My name in my language means Yellow Bird Woman.
I was a banker and a rancher.
I led a lawsuit that won a $3.4 billion settlement for Native Americans.

name: Ed Roberts
bio: Ed Roberts was a pioneering leader of the disability rights movement. He was the first wheelchair user to attend the University of California, Berkeley.
clues: I'm considered a founder of the independent living movement.
I was a pioneer of the disability rights movement.
I was the first wheelchair user to attend UC Berkeley.

name: Edith Windsor
bio: Edith Windsor was a technology manager at IBM and an LGBTQ+ rights activist. At age 83 she won the 2013 Supreme Court case United States v. Windsor, a landmark victory for same-sex marriage.
clues: I worked as a technology manager at IBM.
I won a Supreme Court case when I was 83.
My case, United States v. Windsor, was a landmark win for same-sex marriage.

name: Audre Lorde
bio: Audre Lorde was a poet, writer and activist who described herself as “Black, lesbian, feminist, socialist, mother, warrior, poet.” She co-founded Kitchen Table: Women of Color Press.
clues: I was born Audrey, but I dropped the “y” as a child.
I co-founded Kitchen Table: Women of Color Press.
I called myself a “Black, lesbian, feminist, socialist, mother, warrior, poet.”

name: Zaha Hadid
bio: Zaha Hadid was an Iraqi British architect known as the “Queen of Curves” for her flowing, futuristic buildings. Her works include the London Aquatics Centre built for the 2012 Olympics.

photo.commons: Zaha Hadid in Heydar Aliyev Cultural center in Baku nov 2013 (cropped).jpg

clues: I studied mathematics before I studied architecture.
I used painting as a tool to design buildings.
I was born in Baghdad and designed the London Aquatics Centre for the 2012 Olympics.

name: Ahmed Zewail
bio: Ahmed Zewail was an Egyptian American chemist at Caltech known as the “father of femtochemistry,” the study of chemical reactions that happen in quadrillionths of a second. In 1999 he became the first Arab scientist to win a Nobel Prize in a science field.

photo.commons: Ahmed Zewail HD2009 Othmer Gold Medal portrait.JPG

clues: I was a professor of chemistry and physics at Caltech.
I studied chemical reactions that happen in a tiny fraction of a second.

name: Mona Hanna
bio: Dr. Mona Hanna is a pediatrician whose research exposed the Flint water crisis, when children in Flint, Michigan, were exposed to lead in their drinking water. She wrote the book What the Eyes Don't See and started Rx Kids, a program giving cash support to new families.
clues: I wrote a book called What the Eyes Don't See.
I started a program that gives cash support to babies' families.
My research proved that children in Flint, Michigan, were being poisoned by lead in their water.

name: Naguib Mahfouz
bio: Naguib Mahfouz was an Egyptian writer who published 35 novels and hundreds of short stories over a 70-year career. In 1988 he became the only Egyptian to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.
clues: All of my novels are set in Egypt.
My most famous work is The Cairo Trilogy.
I'm the only Egyptian to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.

name: Hamdi Ulukaya
bio: Hamdi Ulukaya is a Kurdish businessman from Turkey who founded the yogurt company Chobani after buying an old, closed factory in upstate New York. He is known for hiring refugees and supporting refugee causes.
clues: My father advised me to start a small feta cheese factory.
In 2005 I bought a closed-down factory in upstate New York.
I founded the yogurt company Chobani.

name: Rami Malek
bio: Rami Malek is an actor born in California to Egyptian immigrant parents. He won the 2019 Academy Award for Best Actor for playing Freddie Mercury in Bohemian Rhapsody, the first actor of Egyptian heritage to win that award.
clues: I played the hacker Elliot Alderson on Mr. Robot.
I acted in the Night at the Museum movies.
I won an Oscar for playing Freddie Mercury of the band Queen.

name: Lynn Conway
bio: Lynn Conway was a computer scientist and engineer whose inventions shaped how modern computer chips are designed. She restarted her career and became a University of Michigan professor and an advocate for transgender people.

I co-led a revolution in microchip design at Xerox PARC.
IBM fired me for being transgender in 1968 and apologized in 2020.

name: Schuyler Bailar
bio: Schuyler Bailar is a swimmer, author and advocate who swam for Harvard. He was the first openly transgender swimmer in NCAA Division I and the first transgender man to compete as a man in any Division I sport.
clues: Harvard recruited me to swim before I transitioned.
I chose to swim on Harvard's men's team.
I was the first openly transgender NCAA Division I swimmer.

name: Elliot Page
bio: Elliot Page is a Canadian actor, producer and LGBTQ+ rights activist. He was nominated for an Academy Award for the film Juno and has also starred in Inception and the X-Men films.
clues: I played Kitty Pryde in the X-Men movies.
I starred in the movie Inception.
I'm a Canadian actor who was nominated for an Oscar for Juno.

name: Nicole Maines
bio: As a student, Nicole Maines won a 2014 case before Maine's highest court, the first state court ruling that transgender students must be allowed to use the school bathroom matching their gender identity. name: Layshia Clarendon
bio: Layshia Clarendon played eleven seasons in the WNBA. They were the league's first openly transgender and nonbinary player.

I played in the WNBA.

name: Asia Kate Dillon
bio: Asia Kate Dillon is an actor known for Orange Is the New Black and Billions. Their character Taylor Mason on Billions was the first nonbinary main character on North American television.

clues: I played Brandy Epps on Orange Is the New Black.
